en: Poor Aychürök, the woman—
There was no end to her widow’s grief.
If seven khans’ black foes had come,
He would have charged in, coat flying loose,
Raised a mighty battle cry,
And torn her free from them;
But skillful Külchoro was not there.
There was no champion girded for action,
No refuge in which to fortify themselves,
No renowned lion of a noble hero.
What is here today is gone tomorrow—
Such filth this world proves to be!
The black roan with the scanty mane,
Whom he used to mount for holy war,
That honored swift steed was gone;
The kinsman he had led and made a hero,
Whom he had made equal to his own son—
There was no brother left,
Save the wretch Kanchoro.
From the iron-gated stronghold
The Jediger ran shouting;
That puffed-up lion Kanchoro
Showed the look of an enemy.
Here is how it became plain:
He drew his bow like pouring rain,
That wretch shot arrows like hail.
Then see the rain, see the arrows!
Into the white palace,
See the arrows strike in showers;
See the embers burning through the haze;
See the arrows strike without breaking!
Still unbroken, shouting, they surged forward—
See the host that flooded in!
Aychürök’s tower—
Do not ask what befell the tower.
Her face changed, her heart burned;
Your distraught sister-in-law could not stay still.
She wished to die, yet could not die;
Alas, she could not take her own life!
Aychürök wept in bitter resentment:
“My black eyes have gone blind;
Surely God has struck my wretched bloodline.
My cherished younger brother Külchoro—
Surely God has struck down my protector.
Yesterday, when I told him to stop, he would not listen;
When he braced himself with courage,
When I warned him what would happen, he would not listen.
When he whipped and beat
Me, the wretched woman—
Curse this womanhood of mine!—
And I shrieked and cursed him,
Did my curse strike true?
Has what I said truly come to pass?
Has God punished me beyond all others?
Wishing that my curse would fall into water,
I spat into black water;
From the fury of my curse
The black water dried away.
Wishing my curse to prove false,
I spat upon a black stone;
Unable to withstand it, the black stone
Split clean apart.
It seems my curse struck like a whip;
It seems the leopard sultan has died;
It seems God has punished me openly;
It seems my noble lord has died;
It seems the enemy has swarmed upon us!”
Poor Aychürök, the woman,
Lost heart and came apart;
The tears poured from her eyes.
Those dear eyes like a quail’s
Shed tear after separate tear;
Those dear eyes like black currants
Shed tears a whip-length long.
“My bloodthirsty lord!” she shrieked,
And sobbed until she wept blood.
“How can I live without the sultan?”
The proud beauty screamed;
Weeping blood, she lamented,
And Aychürök stood there wailing.
When she saw the enemy’s siege,
Her black hair untouched by comb
She tore out strand by strand;
Her black hair untouched by braid
She flung across her breast.
Her white face, like the risen moon—
Curse this womanhood of hers!—
She clawed open through the middle.
Her hair thinned like meadow grass;
The blood flowing down both cheeks
Poured across her breast.
Upon the woman plunged into mourning,
The enemy surged ravenously.
Her close-fitting dress and quilted coat
Were torn apart like saddle straps;
Her dear hair, fine as raw silk,
Was thinned strand by strand.
The tears flowing down both cheeks
Poured over her collarbones;
Blood covered her pallid face,
A film clouded her black eyes.
Every joint in her body shook;
She moaned, wept, and screamed.
Her ten vertebrae and eighty bones
Seemed to separate layer by layer;
Misfortune and grief, great affliction,
Could plainly be seen, if one looked.
Her insides burned into embers;
The gray wolf was gone from the world.
It could be seen that she was left behind;
It could be seen that the massed Jediger
Had surrounded and taken the place.
Whatever the host desired,
When your black-faced sister-in-law looked,
Gray-mottled banners became their standards,
And cries rang from rank to rank;
Pale, hazy banners rose,
And piercing shouts became a tumult.
Around the precious white palace
The forty-two companies thronged;
There was no remedy to be found,
And bitter misery boiled over.
The heroes and lions
Of the Jediger raised
Piercing cries and rallying shouts.
Without looking up or down,
When they came and besieged the stronghold,
Without reckoning that they might die,
Without glancing around them,
The Jediger, eager for plunder,
Did not spare their lives at all;
Their spears bristled,
Their swords flashed,
Their tasseled standards swayed.
All the warriors grew excited:
Their finest drew the bow,
Their most skillful swung the club,
Heroes of powerful build,
Champions who shattered formations,
Bull-necked, with stallion thighs,
Whose grappling crushed the life from men;
They did not retreat even before death,
Nor flee back from a drawn brow.
The loud, deep-chested men
Were at the front of the raid;
Whoever they met, they would chew to pieces,
Tirelessly striking the foe.
Without saying, “I am dead, I give up,”
They advanced straight into the enemy—
Those dear men were at the fore.
The Jediger flooded in,
Their bravest around the edges.
The white palace had lost its standing;
In the hands of the Jediger,
What was there, and what was not?
Their hard men at the edges
Did not flinch when struck by swords;
Their fortunate men behind them
Did not cry out when pierced by spears.
Facing the red blaze,
They shouted and thrust their spears.
They stood face to face,
Clashing and fighting.
There were bold fellows too
Who surged forward when ordered;
Before one could say this or that,
In the time it took to blink,
Before one could utter another word,
They thundered over everything.
Once roused, they pressed to the end;
They cast a fearsome shadow,
Subdued all who faced them,
And plundered without leaving a thing.
Their renowned men were in front:
They could drink and never fill themselves with blood;
Facing a man, they did not leave him alive.
Their courage was great, their venom strong;
Whoever challenged them lost his life.
Broad-chested, wide-breasted,
They had many strapping men.
When a fierce gun cracked,
Many indeed started and fled.
There were also many clumsy men
Who joined the ranks and seized livestock,
Saying, “I too am a son of man,”
When the host was hemmed in.
Though they had tongues, they understood no speech,
And would not simply go where they were driven;
There were calves like those as well.
There were cowards too
Who never stepped outside at night.
An earth-splitting host of ten thousand
Committed dreadful deeds before one’s eyes;
Old women and young brides—
Against all those within the stronghold
They poured in by force.
There was no strength to exchange blows,
No means to grapple with them,
No power left to resist.
God’s sun in the sky was overcast;
Upon widow, orphan, and the weak,
Upon the wretched subjected to torment,
Sixty afflictions came at once.
Their insides burned to embers;
The Jediger surrounded them completely.
The dear Kyrgyz who had settled broad Talas,
Who would not yield a companion’s life,
Were gone.
The Jediger flooded in,
Showing no pity for those dear lives,
Paying no heed
That they were widows and orphans.
They drew bows like pouring rain,
Shot arrows like falling hail;
The musket balls whistled,
The bowstrings’ arrows hissed,
The short guns’ balls glowed red.
They came and struck the palace,
Bullets scattering like hail,
The musket balls plainly visible.
When the Jediger closed in,
Old women and young wives
Had no strength to show courage;
There was no male child of the khan,
No champion girded for action,
No people on whom to rely,
No forest to give them shelter,
No homeland into which to flee.
When God destroys one’s equal,
This world is born as filth indeed.
Its gate was pierced with firing holes;
The keepers at the gate,
Fighting as men who had escaped death,
Fired guns and drew bows,
Clashing together in combat;
Dark blood flowed like water
As they fought to bar the gate.
What could the poor gatekeepers do?
They stood giving ground,
They stood without yielding passage,
Weary beyond all measure.
With steel shafts and sharpened points,
Fletched with black hair,
The bloodthirsty lord had armed the gate
With keen, unsheathed steel.
Men lay sprawled before the gate;
The Jediger’s hearts were crushed,
For those who ventured near the gate
Lay stretched out dead.
The seasoned guards,
Those appointed to keep the gate,
Took up red-steel spears,
Faced outward at every loophole,
Raised battle-axes and spears,
And fired at chosen targets.
